questionText: What is the difference between a fat JAR and a regular JAR in Spring Boot?

target.learningOutcome: The learner can compare a regular application JAR with a Spring Boot executable JAR, identify the BOOT-INF layout, explain the launcher, and avoid confusing nested and shaded packaging.
outOfScope: A claim that every fat JAR contains a server
A claim that the archive contains a Java runtime
A claim that nested and shaded JARs are identical

claims.statement: Spring Boot's build plugin can create executable archives that contain an application's runtime dependencies and can be started with java -jar.
A repackaged Spring Boot JAR stores application classes in BOOT-INF/classes and dependency JARs in BOOT-INF/lib.
The Spring Boot Maven plugin's repackage goal operates on the archive produced by the normal package phase and creates the executable layout.
Spring Boot executable JARs keep dependency JARs nested rather than requiring all dependency classes to be merged into one flat directory.
Layered Boot archives include metadata that lets image-building tools separate categories such as dependencies and application content.

examples.title: Inspect BOOT-INF entries and launch the archive

validation.command: Review jar tf filtering and java -jar invocation against an executable Spring Boot archive
validation.expected: The trace distinguishes BOOT-INF/classes from BOOT-INF/lib and uses the normal executable-JAR launch

visuals.title: Regular application JAR and Spring Boot executable JAR comparison

notes: The lesson uses fat JAR as a familiar term while explicitly distinguishing Boot's nested-JAR layout from flat shading.

review.notes: Executable packaging, BOOT-INF, repackage, launcher, and layered archive claims were checked against the official Boot packaging documentation. The shell trace is manual because it depends on a built artifact.
